q: Which regional planning theory explains the hierarchical arrangement of settlements, whereby larger urban centers provide specialized goods and services to smaller surrounding communities?
o: Urban Realms Model (James E. Vance Jr., 1964/1967)
Multiple Nuclei Theory (Chauncy Harris & Edward Ullman, 1945)
n: Christaller's Central Place Theory (1933) explains a hierarchy of settlements serving smaller surrounding ones. Source: Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: As a city expands from its central business district, urban development occurs in a series of growth rings, with each ring representing a distinct zone of land use and socioeconomic activity Which urban structure model best explains this pattern of development?
o: Urban Realms Model (James E. Vance Jr., 1964/1967)
Multiple Nuclei Theory (Chauncy Harris & Edward Ullman, 1945)
n: Burgess's Concentric Zone Theory (1925) describes growth in rings from the CBD. Source: Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: Which urban planning theory advocates the development of self-contained towns surrounded by greenbelts, where residential, commercial, and civic functions are integrated to balance urban growth with access to nature?
o: Multiple Nuclei Theory (Chauncy Harris & Edward Ullman, 1945)
n: Ebenezer Howard's Garden City (1898) proposes self-contained towns with integrated uses, ringed by greenbelts. Source: Howard, Garden Cities of To-morrow (1902).

q: According to one urban land-use model, cities tend to grow in wedge-shaped sectors radiating outward from the central business district, with transportation corridors often influencing the location of residential, industrial, and commercial districts. Which urban structure model best explains this pattern of development?
o: Urban Realms Model (James E. Vance Jr., 1964/1967)
Multiple Nuclei Theory (Chauncy Harris & Edward Ullman, 1945)
n: Hoyt's Sector Theory (1939) describes wedge-shaped sectors along transport corridors. Source: Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: Which urban planning theory proposes that a metropolitan area is composed of several semi- autonomous regions, each with its own commercial center, employment opportunities, and supporting services?
o: Multiple Nuclei Theory (Chauncy Harris & Edward Ullman, 1945)
Urban Realms Model (James E. Vance Jr., 1964/1967)
n: Vance's Urban Realms Model describes a metropolis of semi-autonomous realms, each with its own center. Source: Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: As a city expands, the traditional single central business district may be supplemented by multiple CBDs, specialized commercial hubs, industrial districts, university zones, and transportation-oriented business centers. These activity areas develop because differ-s* land uses tend to cluster in locations that best support their particular functions. Which t° structure model best explains this pattern of metropolitan growth?
o: Urban Realms Model (James E. Vance Jr., 1964/1967)
Multiple Nuclei Theory (Chauncy Harris & Edward Ullman, 1945)
n: Harris and Ullman's Multiple Nuclei Theory (1945) explains growth around several specialized centers. Source: Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: Which urban planning concept proposed high-rise buildings surrounded by generous open green spaces, with residential, comrrercial, industrial, and civic functions separated through strict land-use zoning?
o: Urban Realms Model (James E. Vance Jr., 1964/1967)
n: Le Corbusier's Radiant City (Ville Radieuse) proposed towers in green space with strictly separated functions. Source: Le Corbusier, La Ville Radieuse (1933); Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: He authored the book Cities in Evolution: An Introduction to the Town Planning Movement and to the Study of Civics.
n: Patrick Geddes wrote Cities in Evolution (1915). Source: Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: At the turn of the 20th century, several planning theories attempted to address overcrowding, pollution, and deteriorating living conditions in rapidly industrializing cities. One influential approach proposed creating self-contained communities separated from the main metropolis, each featuring balanced land uses, ample open space, and a surrounding greenbelt to control urban expansion. Which planning movement introduced this concept?
n: The Garden City Movement proposed self-contained towns ringed by greenbelts. Source: Howard, Garden Cities of To-morrow.

q: The Garden City Movement was a 20th-century urban planning movement which promoted the idea of satellite communities surrounding the central city with greenbelts as separation. The garden cities would contain proportionate areas of residences, industry and agriculture. Who led this movement?
n: Ebenezer Howard founded the Garden City Movement with To-morrow: A Peaceful Path to Real Reform (1898). This led to Letchworth and Welwyn Garden City. Source: Howard, Garden Cities of To-morrow.

q: An American urban planner known for his work on the perceptual form of urban environments and was an early advocate of mental mapping. He is the author of The Image of the City which posted that observers take in information of the city and use it to make mental maps of their surroundings. Contributing to these mental images are Paths, Edges, Districts, Nodes and Landmark
n: Kevin Lynch wrote The Image of the City (1960): paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks. Source: Lynch, The Image of the City.

q: Which architect followed Ebenezer Howard's Garden City ideals and later became a leading figure in British town planning, authoring influential planning texts and serving as Chief Town Planning Adviser to the government?
n: Raymond Unwin, who followed Howard and planned Letchworth, became Chief Town Planning Adviser and wrote Town Planning in Practice. Source: Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: Which ancient Greek figure is recognized as the first known urban planner—credited with introducing the gridiron street layout and functional zoning (sacred, public, and private areas) in cities such as Piraeus, and whose rational approach to civic organization influenced Roman and Renaissance planning models?
n: Hippodamus of Miletus is the first known urban planner, credited with the grid and zoned planning at Piraeus. Source: Aristotle, Politics II.8; Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: Who is considered the father of modern urban planning—known for introducing the "Survey–Analysis–Plan" method, promoting ecological and sociological integration in city design, and emphasizing the relationship between place, work, and folk in shaping livable environments?
n: Patrick Geddes, father of modern planning, introduced "Survey–Analysis–Plan" and the triad of place, work and folk. Source: Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: A principle of good space planning that is flexible and adapts to user needs.
n: Flexibility means spaces adapt to changing user needs. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order; Karlen, Space Planning Basics.

q: A principle of good space planning that tailors spaces to different functions.
n: User-centric planning tailors spaces to their functions and users. Source: Karlen, Space Planning Basics.

q: It refers to the circulation systems within a city which connect different parts of the city and facilitate movement.
n: Paths are the circulation channels connecting parts of a city. Source: Lynch, The Image of the City.

q: It refers to the distinct areas within a city, often defined by their land use patterns, cultural or economic characteristics, or history.
n: Districts are distinct areas defined by use, culture, economy or history. Source: Lynch, The Image of the City.

q: It refers to the intersection of paths or the active areas within a city such as squares, plazas or transportation hubs.
n: Nodes are intersections and focal points such as squares, plazas and transit hubs. Source: Lynch, The Image of the City.

q: It refers to the distinctive features within a city that help define its identity, such as monuments, iconic buildings, or natural features. It is a point of reference.
n: Landmarks are distinctive reference points such as monuments, iconic buildings and natural features. Source: Lynch, The Image of the City.

q: This Greek architect and urban planner was known as the father of Ekistics which concerns the multi-aspect science of human settlements, including regional, city, Community planning and dwelling design. He made the insightful observation that "The big mistake most commonly made today is that when we speak of transportation we think only af persons and goods. We forget the wht 367 existence of water, clean or otherwise, moving in pipes, of gas, oil, electricity, messages, the telephones, etc. The result is that we waste a lot of space and networks.
n: Constantinos Doxiadis founded Ekistics, the science of human settlements. Source: Doxiadis, Ekistics (1968).

q: Inthe science of human settlements (ekistics), which element refers to the phys. —. environment—including land, water, climate, and natural resources—upon which settles, are built and within which they operate?
n: In ekistics, Nature is the physical environment of land, water, climate and resources. Source: Doxiadis, Ekistics (five elements: Nature, Man, Society, Shells, Networks).

q: Inthe framework of ekistics, which element refers to the organized structure of human relationships—including culture, economy, governance, and institutions—that shape the way people live together in settlements?
n: In ekistics, Society is the organized structure of human relations: culture, economy, governance. Source: Doxiadis, Ekistics.

q: The main purpose of the County of London Plan of 1943 was to point out the main directions of development for London in anticipation of the end of World War Jl and the reconstruction of London after extensive bomb damage and to solve the problem of the large movements of the populace. The proponents of this plan was John Henry Forshaw and _ _.
n: The 1943 County of London Plan was by J.H. Forshaw and Sir Patrick Abercrombie. Source: Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: A type of city plan in which streets run at right angles to each other. Wayfinding is very easy under this plan, but it has the disadvantage of traffic congestion.
n: Gridiron plans have streets at right angles. Wayfinding is easy, but traffic tends to congest. Source: Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: Roads under this city pattern are connected by radiating roads. The business area is typically located at the core and the industrial area is interspersed within the residential. The periphery has greenbelts. It has the advantage of a direct line of travel and easier flow of traffic; the disadvantage is central congestion.
n: Concentric (radial-ring) plans have radiating roads, a central business core and peripheral greenbelts. Their drawback is central congestion. Source: Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: Urban land-use patterns have been interpreted through several foundational models. One theory proposes that land uses do not expand in uniform rings but instead develop in directional wedges influenced by transportation corridors, environmental amenities, and socio-economic clustering. This mode} argues that cities grow outward along sectors rather than concentric circles, Which urban model is described by this wedge-shaped pattern of development?
n: The Sector Model describes wedge-shaped growth along transport corridors. Source: Hoyt (1939); Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: Urban spatial structure has been interpreted through several classical theories. One perspective argues that cities do not expand in uniform rings or directional wedges. Instead, development emerged around separate activity areas, each shaped by land-use compatibility, clustering of related functions, and the tendency of certain activities to locate away from others. This results in a pattern where different zones form around distinct functional centers rather than a single dominant core. Which urban mode! best explains this pattern of development?
n: The Multiple Nuclei Model describes growth around separate functional centers. Source: Harris & Ullman (1945); Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: It refers to a linear geographical area that facilitates the movement of people, goods or wildlife. It often centers around transportation infrastructure such as streets, highways and public transit systems, but can also include natural features like rivers or historic sites.
n: A corridor is a linear area for moving people, goods or wildlife, along roads, transit, rivers or heritage routes. Source: Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: Which planning concept refers to a zone of protected open land surrounding urban areas, designed to limit urban sprawl, preserve natural habitats, and provide recreational spaces?
n: A greenbelt is protected open land around a city that limits sprawl and preserves habitat and recreation. Source: Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: An urban plan for an elongated urban formation. The city would consist of a series of functionally specialized Parallel sectors. As the city expands, additional sectors would be added to the end of each band, making the city longer without growing wider. Main disadvantage would be its sensitivity to block age.
n: A linear city is a long band of parallel specialized strips that grows at its ends. It is vulnerable to blockage. Source: Soria y Mata, Ciudad Lineal; Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: A desired road for those who desire silence and privacy; a dead end.
n: A cul-de-sac is a dead-end street giving quiet and privacy. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: Focuses on cities or densely populated areas. Organizes land use, transportation, housing, infrastructure and public spaces. It covers challenges like population density, traffic congestion, housing shortages and sustainable develoomaent. [t includes planning for metro systems, zoning laws, or renewal projects in major cities.
n: Urban planning covers cities: land use, transport, housing, infrastructure, public space, zoning and renewal. Source: Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: Centers on smaller towns or suburban areas with less population density than cities. It ensures efficient development by balancing residential, commercial and public spaces often addressing localized needs such as creating a harmonious blend of housing, parks and roads in a smaller are. It includes developing a master plan for a growing suburban area.
n: Town planning covers smaller towns and suburbs, balancing residential, commercial and public space. Source: Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: It encompasses a large geographical area which can include multiple cities and rural areas, coordinating development across such areas to address economic, environmental and infrastructural issues on a broader scale. It focuses on connectivity, disaster resilience, resource management and equitable development.
n: Regional planning coordinates development across several cities and rural areas, including water, transport and resilience. Source: Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: It typically focuses on specific neighborhoods within a town or city. It aims to empower residents to shape their environment by addressing social needs, public amenities and local resources, including participatory processes in decisions about schools, parks, safety or cultural spaces.
n: Community planning focuses on neighborhoods and empowers residents through participatory processes. Source: Hall, Urban and Regional Planning; LeGates & Stout, The City Reader.

q: The first row houses in America were located in
n: America's first row houses are in Philadelphia; Elfreth's Alley dates from the early 1700s. Source: National Park Service, Elfreth's Alley NHL.

q: It determines the visual weight of the design, establishes space and perspective, and often resolves where the eye goes first when looking at a design: the focal point.
n: Emphasis sets visual weight and the focal point, deciding where the eye goes first. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order.

q: The difference between elements within a work of art or composition
n: Contrast is the difference between elements in a composition. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order.

q: The darkness or lightness of color
n: Value is the lightness or darkness of a color. Source: Munsell color system; Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order.

q: What is the darkness of an object not in direct light?
n: Shade is the darkness of a surface turned away from direct light. A shadow is cast on another surface. Source: Ching, Architectural Graphics (shade and shadow).

q: It focuses on balancing individual elements to create pleasing relationships, like consistent materials and proportions. It is about the parts.
n: Harmony balances individual elements so their relationships please, through consistent materials and proportions. It concerns the parts. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order.

q: It emphasizes wholeness, ensuring all components align with a single cohesive concept. It is about the overall design.
n: Unity is wholeness: every component aligned to one cohesive concept. It concerns the overall design. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order.

q: Looking at the complex of the Salk Institute, designed by Louis Kahn, what is prevalent?
n: Kahn's Salk Institute is strongly symmetrical: two mirrored laboratory wings on a central plaza and axis. Source: ; Salk Institute.

q: In architectural composition and site planning, designers often aim for a sense of order, stability, and formal clarity by arranging elements so that both sides of a space or form correspond in shape, proportion, and placement relative to an axis. Which design principle is being applied?
n: Matching both sides about an axis in shape, proportion and placement is symmetry. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order.

q: In architectural composition, designers often arrange forms, spaces, and visual elements so that the overall composition feels intentional and cohesive. This approach relies on distributing visual components in a way that supports a unified reading of the design. Which design principle is being applied?
n: Distributing visual components so the composition feels intentional and cohesive is balance. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order.

q: What is the identifying characteristic of a volume, determined by the shapes and interrelationships of the planes?
n: The shapes of a volume's planes and their interrelationships give it its form. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order, Ch. 2.
